correctness.rationale: The proof is structurally sound. If a proper closed convex \(F\) contains \(a+V\), convexity gives \(x+v+t(a-x)\in F\) and closedness gives \(F+V=F\); quotienting by the hyperplane direction makes \(F\) the inverse image of a closed interval. Two distinct hyperplane directions would span all of \(\mathbb R^d\), forcing \(F=\mathbb R^d\), so proper members have unique direction. A face cannot mix distinct proper directions. Within one direction, the complex is the nerve of intervals; deleting an interval with minimal finite right endpoint is a valid elementary 1-collapse, and the all-right-unbounded remainder is a simplex. Universal vertices only join the unique maximal face and can be removed last.
residual_risks: The argument is specific to codimension one and does not extend directly to smaller \(k\).

The audited codimension-one proof uses a special structural collapse unavailable in lower codimension: every proper closed convex set containing a hyperplane is a generalized slab with one normal line, so each direction block becomes an interval nerve. Resultary and web searches found the audited record as the exact match and no older codimension-one theorem. Best-of-knowledge originality therefore passes, with an explicit access limitation on the primary paper.
